lessons.title: When and how to remove grafting tape without damaging the graft
lessons.body:
Grafting tape holds the scion and rootstock tightly together so the cambium layers can fuse. But if you leave it on too long, it can girdle the tree, cutting off water and nutrients. In most African conditions, remove the tape once the graft has taken and new growth is 10â15 cm long. This usually happens 4â8 weeks after grafting, depending on the species and season. For mango, wait 6â8 weeks; for citrus, 4â6 weeks; for avocado, 8â10 weeks. Check weekly by looking for green shoots emerging from the scion. If the scion is still green and plump, the graft is alive. If it shrivels or turns brown, it failedâremove the tape anyway and regraft later.

To remove tape, use a sharp, clean knife or razor blade. Do not pull the tape offâyou might tear the tender callus tissue. Instead, cut the tape lengthwise along the side of the graft, away from the bud or shoot. For plastic tape, make a single cut and peel it back gently. For biodegradable tape, you can leave it if it breaks down within 3 months, but check regularly. If the tape is stuck to the bark, moisten it with water for 10 minutes before cutting.

After removal, inspect the graft union. It should look like a smooth, slightly swollen seam. If you see any constriction marks, the tape was left too longâthe tree may recover, but watch for weak growth. Do not remove tape on a windy day; the graft is fragile. If you must remove tape early because of girdling, do it in the cool of the evening and provide shade for a few days.

In dry areas like the Sahel, tape can dry and crack, falling off on its own. In humid areas like the Congo Basin, tape may rot and attract fungus. After removal, spray the graft union with a copper-based fungicide (e.g., copper oxychloride at 3 g per litre) to prevent infection. Always sterilise your knife with methylated spirits or fire between trees to avoid spreading disease.

lessons.title: Managing water and shade for newly grafted trees
lessons.body:
New grafts are like newborn babiesâthey need consistent moisture and protection from harsh sun. For the first 2 weeks after grafting, water the rootstock every 2â3 days if there is no rain. Give 5â10 litres per tree, depending on soil type. Sandy soils dry out faster, so water daily in hot weather. Clay soils hold water, so every 3â4 days is enough. Never let the soil dry out completely, but do not waterlog itâroots need air. A simple test: dig 10 cm down; if the soil feels like a wrung-out cloth, it's perfect. If it's bone dry, water. If it's soggy, wait.

Shade is critical. Direct sun can cook a tender graft. In open fields, build a shade structure using palm fronds, banana leaves, or shade net (50% shade). Place it on the sunny side, about 50 cm above the graft. For a single tree, a simple tripod of sticks with a thatch roof works. In agroforestry systems, plant living shade like pigeon pea or moringa 1â2 metres away, but prune them so they don't compete for water. Remove shade gradually over 3â4 weeks once new leaves are firm and dark green. Sudden exposure can scorch them.

Mulching is your best friend. Spread a 5â10 cm layer of dry grass, straw, or maize stover around the base, but keep it 5 cm away from the trunk to prevent rot. Mulch reduces evaporation by up to 70% and keeps soil temperature stable. In very hot areas, water in the early morning or late evening to reduce loss. If you have drip irrigation, run it for 30 minutes daily. Otherwise, use a watering can or bucket.

During the rainy season, ensure good drainageâdig a shallow channel if water pools. Too much water causes root rot, which kills grafts faster than drought. After 4â6 weeks, when the graft is established, reduce watering to once a week, but increase amount to 15â20 litres. Always check the graft union for signs of stress: wilting leaves, brown tips, or cracks. Adjust water and shade accordingly.

lessons.title: Fertilizing young grafts with locally available organic matter
lessons.body:
Young grafts need gentle, balanced nutritionânot a heavy dose of chemical fertilizer that can burn tender roots. Start fertilizing 4â6 weeks after grafting, once new shoots are 10â15 cm long. Use well-rotted manure, compost, or kitchen ash. For each tree, apply 2â3 handfuls (about 200â300 g) of compost or aged cow dung. Spread it in a ring 15â20 cm from the trunk, then cover with a thin layer of soil. Do not pile it against the stemâit invites termites and rot.

If you have poultry manure, use lessâone handful (100 g) per tree, because it is strong. Mix it with wood ash (a source of potassium) at a ratio of 3:1. For phosphorus, crush bones from your kitchen, burn them, and grind into powder. Add one tablespoon (10 g) per tree. For potassium, banana peels and wood ash are excellent. Soak banana peels in water for a week, then pour the liquid around the tree. This 'banana tea' also adds minor nutrients.

In many African soils, nitrogen is low. Plant leguminous cover crops like cowpea, groundnut, or lablab between your trees. They fix nitrogen from the air. When they flower, cut them and leave the residues as mulch. This slowly releases nitrogen. Alternatively, make a liquid fertilizer: fill a sack with fresh animal manure (cow, goat, or chicken), tie it, and soak in a 200-litre drum of water for 2 weeks. Dilute 1 part tea to 3 parts water and apply 2 litres per tree every 2 weeks.

Do not fertilize during the dry season when the tree is dormantâwait for the rains. Also, avoid fresh manure; it heats up and burns roots. If leaves are yellow, add a bit more nitrogen (e.g., urine diluted 1:10). If leaves are dark green but few flowers later, reduce nitrogen and add ash. Always water after applying any fertilizer. Keep records of what you apply and whenâthis helps you learn what works in your area.

lessons.title: Controlling pests and diseases on new grafts
lessons.body:
New grafts are vulnerable to pests and diseases because their tissues are soft and wounds are open. Scout your trees twice a week. Look for holes in leaves, sticky sap, curled shoots, or powdery spots. Common pests include aphids, whiteflies, mealybugs, and termites. Aphids cluster on new shoots and suck sap. Spray with a soap solution: mix 1 tablespoon of liquid soap in 1 litre of water, add a pinch of chilli powder, and spray in the evening. Repeat every 3 days until gone. For whiteflies, yellow sticky traps workâpaint a piece of cardboard yellow, coat with grease, and hang near the tree.

Termites are a major threat in dry savannahs. They attack the graft union and roots. To prevent, keep the area around the tree clean of dead wood. Apply wood ash in a ring around the base. If you see termite mounds nearby, destroy them or pour a mixture of Neem oil and water (10 ml per litre) into the mound. For active infestations, use a bait of cardboard soaked in insecticide (e.g., fipronil) placed near the mound, but handle chemicals carefully.

Diseases like powdery mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial wilt often appear in humid conditions. Powdery mildew looks like white flour on leaves. Spray with a baking soda solution: 1 teaspoon baking soda, 1 litre water, a few drops of soap. For anthracnose (dark sunken spots on leaves and stems), remove infected parts and burn them. Spray copper fungicide (3 g per litre) every 10 days. Bacterial wilt causes sudden wiltingâthere is no cure, so remove and burn the tree to save others.

Prevention is better than cure. Keep tools clean. Avoid overhead watering, which spreads spores. Plant resistant rootstocks if available. Encourage natural enemies like ladybirds and spiders by planting flowers such as marigolds and sunflowers nearby. If you must use chemical pesticides, choose those with low toxicity, like neem-based products, and follow label instructions. Never spray during flowering to protect bees.

lessons.title: Training the new shoot into a strong tree structure
lessons.body:
Once your graft has produced a strong shoot (30â40 cm tall), you need to train it into a tree that will bear heavy crops without breaking. The goal is a single, straight trunk with well-spaced branches. Start by removing any shoots that grow from the rootstock below the graft unionâthese are suckers and will steal nutrients. Cut them cleanly with a sharp knife when they are small (less than 10 cm). Check weekly.

If the main shoot is growing sideways, tie it to a straight stick (bamboo or eucalyptus) using soft cloth or banana fibre. Do not use wireâit cuts the bark. Loosen the tie every month as the stem thickens. For fruit trees like mango, avocado, and citrus, aim for a central leader (one main stem) with 3â5 side branches. When the main stem reaches 60â80 cm, pinch off the tip to encourage branching. This is called 'heading'. Choose side branches that are spaced 15â20 cm apart and point outward at a wide angle (45â60 degrees). Remove branches that grow inward or rub against others.

In the first year, remove flowers and fruits. This feels wasteful, but it lets the tree put energy into roots and branches. For example, pluck off all mango flowers in the first season. In the second year, allow a few fruits to test, but still remove most. By the third year, you can let it bear normally. For grafted trees, the rootstock may send up vigorous shootsâremove them promptly, or they will dominate.

Prune during the dry season when growth is slow, using clean, sharp secateurs. Make cuts at a slight angle, just above a bud, facing outward. Seal large cuts (bigger than 2 cm) with pruning paint or mud to prevent disease. Train your tree to a open centre or vase shape for easy harvesting and good air flow. This reduces fungal diseases. Always step back and look at the tree from all sidesâimagine a bird flying through it. If branches block the centre, remove them. A well-trained tree lives longer and yields more.

lessons.title: Hands-on: Inspecting and caring for your grafts after 2 weeks
lessons.body:
Two weeks after grafting, it's time for a thorough inspection. Grab your notebook, a sharp knife, and a roll of grafting tape in case you need to rewrap. Walk to your tree in the morning when it's cool. First, look at the scion. Is it still green and plump? If yes, the graft is likely alive. If it's shrivelled, brown, or black, it has failed. Use your fingernail to gently scratch the bark of the scionâif you see green underneath, it's alive. If it's brown and dry, remove the tape and cut the scion off cleanly. You can regraft on the same rootstock if it's healthy.

Next, check the graft union. Gently feel for swellingâthat's callus tissue forming. Do not poke or prod too much. Look for any signs of rot, mould, or insect damage. If you see white cottony masses, that's mealybugs. Dab them with a cotton bud dipped in methylated spirits. If the union looks dry and cracked, wrap a new layer of grafting tape around it, but not too tight. Water the tree if the soil is dry. If it's been raining heavily, check for waterlogged soil and improve drainage.

Remove any shoots growing from the rootstock below the graft. These are easy to spotâthey grow fast and have different leaves. Cut them off at the base. Also remove any weeds within 30 cm of the trunk; they compete for water and nutrients. Apply a handful of compost or well-rotted manure in a ring around the tree, then water it in. If you have shade netting, make sure it's still in place and not touching the leaves.

Record everything in your notebook: date, scion condition, union appearance, pests seen, actions taken. Take a photo if you can. This record helps you track progress and spot problems early. If the graft has taken, you'll see new leaves unfolding in the next week. If not, plan to regraft in the next season. Remember, aftercare is the difference between a successful graft and a dead stick. Keep observing weekly until the shoot is at least 30 cm tall.

quiz.q: How long should you generally wait before removing grafting tape from a mango graft?
quiz.explanation: Mango grafts typically take 6â8 weeks to heal sufficiently before tape removal.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to remove grafting tape?
options: B) Cut it lengthwise and peel gently
quiz.explanation: Cutting lengthwise avoids tearing the tender callus tissue at the graft union.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid removing grafting tape on a windy day?
options: A) The tape may blow away
B) The graft is fragile and can break
quiz.explanation: Wind can snap the newly healed graft union if the tape is removed.

quiz.q: What should you do if the scion is shrivelled and brown when you check the graft?
options: B) Remove tape and regraft later
quiz.explanation: A shrivelled brown scion indicates graft failure; remove tape and plan to regraft.

quiz.q: How often should you water a newly grafted tree in sandy soil during hot weather?
quiz.explanation: Sandy soils dry out quickly, so daily watering is needed in hot conditions.

quiz.q: What is the ideal shade percentage for a new graft?
quiz.explanation: 50% shade net or thatch provides protection without completely blocking light.

quiz.q: How can you test if soil moisture is adequate for a new graft?
options: A) Dig 10 cm down and feel the soil
quiz.explanation: Feeling soil at 10 cm depth gives a reliable indication of moisture.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of mulching around a new graft?
options: B) Reduces evaporation and stabilizes temperature
quiz.explanation: Mulch conserves water and buffers soil temperature extremes.

quiz.q: When should you start fertilizing a young graft?
options: B) 4â6 weeks after new shoots appear
quiz.explanation: Fertilizing too early can burn tender roots; wait until new growth is established.

quiz.q: Which local material is a good source of potassium for young grafts?
quiz.explanation: Wood ash is rich in potassium and other minerals.

quiz.q: How should you apply compost around a young graft?
options: A) Pile it against the trunk
B) Spread in a ring 15â20 cm from the trunk
quiz.explanation: Keeping compost away from the trunk prevents rot and termite damage.

quiz.q: What is 'banana tea' used for?
options: B) Providing potassium and minor nutrients
quiz.explanation: Soaking banana peels in water releases potassium and other nutrients.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid fertilizing during the dry season?
options: A) Trees are dormant and may not absorb nutrients
quiz.explanation: Dry season dormancy means roots are less active; fertilizer can burn them.

quiz.q: Which pest clusters on new shoots and sucks sap?
quiz.explanation: Aphids are common sap-sucking pests on tender new growth.

quiz.q: What is a simple homemade spray for aphids?
quiz.explanation: Soap and chilli disrupt aphid feeding and repel them.

quiz.q: How can you prevent termite attack on grafts?
options: A) Keep area clear of dead wood and apply wood ash
quiz.explanation: Removing dead wood and applying wood ash creates an unfavorable environment for termites.

quiz.q: What does powdery mildew look like?
options: A) White flour-like coating on leaves
quiz.explanation: Powdery mildew appears as a white powdery growth on leaf surfaces.

quiz.q: Which fungicide can be used for anthracnose?
quiz.explanation: Copper-based fungicides are effective against anthracnose.

quiz.q: Why should you remove suckers from the rootstock?
options: B) They compete for nutrients and can dominate the graft
quiz.explanation: Suckers divert resources from the grafted scion and can overtake it.

quiz.q: What is 'heading' in training a young tree?
options: A) Removing the top tip to encourage branching
quiz.explanation: Heading involves pinching off the terminal bud to promote side branches.

quiz.q: Why should you remove flowers and fruits in the first year after grafting?
options: A) To let the tree put energy into roots and branches
quiz.explanation: Early fruit removal allows vegetative growth to establish a strong framework.

quiz.q: What is the ideal angle for side branches on a young fruit tree?
quiz.explanation: Wide angles (45â60 degrees) create stronger branch attachments.

quiz.q: When is the best time to prune a young grafted tree?
quiz.explanation: Dry season pruning reduces disease risk and slows growth less.

quiz.q: How should you seal a large pruning cut?
options: A) With mud or pruning paint
quiz.explanation: Sealing cuts prevents disease entry and desiccation.

quiz.q: What should you check for when inspecting a graft after 2 weeks?
quiz.explanation: A thorough inspection covers scion health, union healing, and pest/disease signs.

quiz.q: How can you tell if a scion is still alive?
options: A) Scratch the bark and look for green
quiz.explanation: Green tissue under the bark indicates living cambium.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see mealybugs on a new graft?
quiz.explanation: Methylated spirits on a cotton bud kills mealybugs on contact.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep records of graft aftercare?
options: A) To track progress and learn what works
quiz.explanation: Records help you identify successful practices and early problems.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a graft has taken successfully?
options: A) New leaves unfolding from the scion
quiz.explanation: New growth from the scion indicates the graft union is functioning.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect grafts during the first month?
quiz.explanation: Frequent inspection (twice weekly) allows early detection of problems.
